claim: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is a collection of neural cells contained in the wall of the gut.
source: The enteric nervous system (ENS), a collection of neural cells contained in the wall of the gut, is of fundamental importance to gastrointestinal and systemic health.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes what the ENS is.

claim: The ENS is of fundamental importance to gastrointestinal and systemic health.
source: The enteric nervous system (ENS), a collection of neural cells contained in the wall of the gut, is of fundamental importance to gastrointestinal and systemic health.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding about the importance of the ENS.

claim: According to the prevailing paradigm, the ENS arises from progenitor cells migrating from the neural crest.
source: According to the prevailing paradigm, the ENS arises from progenitor cells migrating from the neural crest and remains largely unchanged thereafter.
evidence: This describes the existing scientific paradigm that the study challenges.

claim: The lineage composition of maturing ENS changes with time, with a decline in the canonical lineage of neural-crest derived neurons.
source: Here, we show that the lineage composition of maturing ENS changes with time, with a decline in the canonical lineage of neural-crest derived neurons and their replacement by a newly identified lineage of mesoderm-derived neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural-crest derived neurons are replaced by a newly identified lineage of mesoderm-derived neurons.
source: Here, we show that the lineage composition of maturing ENS changes with time, with a decline in the canonical lineage of neural-crest derived neurons and their replacement by a newly identified lineage of mesoderm-derived neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by lineage tracing experiments and immunochemical data.

claim: Single cell transcriptomics and immunochemical approaches establish a distinct expression profile of mesoderm-derived neurons.
source: Single cell transcriptomics and immunochemical approaches establish a distinct expression profile of mesoderm-derived neurons.
evidence: This describes the methodological approaches used to characterize MENs, with results shown in Figures 4-5.

claim: The dynamic balance between the proportions of neurons from neural-crest and mesoderm lineages in the post-natal gut is dependent on the availability of GDNF-RET and HGF-MET trophic signals.
source: The dynamic balance between the proportions of neurons from these two different lineages in the post-natal gut is dependent on the availability of their respective trophic signals, GDNF-RET and HGF-MET.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of GDNF and HGF supplementation on neuronal populations.

claim: With increasing age, mesoderm-derived neurons become the dominant form of neurons in the ENS.
source: With increasing age, the mesoderm-derived neurons become the dominant form of neurons in the ENS, a change associated with significant functional effects on intestinal motility which can be reversed by GDNF supplementation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification data in Figure 10 showing age-dependent changes in neuronal lineage proportions.

claim: The age-associated change in neuronal lineage composition is associated with significant functional effects on intestinal motility.
source: With increasing age, the mesoderm-derived neurons become the dominant form of neurons in the ENS, a change associated with significant functional effects on intestinal motility which can be reversed by GDNF supplementation.
evidence: This is supported by whole gut transit time measurements in aged mice shown in Figure 13.

claim: The functional effects on intestinal motility can be reversed by GDNF supplementation.
source: With increasing age, the mesoderm-derived neurons become the dominant form of neurons in the ENS, a change associated with significant functional effects on intestinal motility which can be reversed by GDNF supplementation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 13 showing improved transit times after GDNF treatment.

claim: Patients with intestinal dysmotility show reduced GDNF-RET signaling in human gut tissues.
source: Transcriptomic analyses of human gut tissues show reduced GDNF-RET signaling in patients with intestinal dysmotility which is associated with reduction in neural crest-derived neuronal markers and concomitant increase in transcriptional patterns specific to mesoderm-derived neurons.
evidence: This is based on analysis of publicly available transcriptomic data from patients with obstructed defecation shown in Figure 14.

claim: Reduced GDNF-RET signaling in patients with intestinal dysmotility is associated with reduction in neural crest-derived neuronal markers.
source: Transcriptomic analyses of human gut tissues show reduced GDNF-RET signaling in patients with intestinal dysmotility which is associated with reduction in neural crest-derived neuronal markers and concomitant increase in transcriptional patterns specific to mesoderm-derived neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 14b.

claim: Reduced GDNF-RET signaling in patients with intestinal dysmotility is associated with increase in transcriptional patterns specific to mesoderm-derived neurons.
source: Transcriptomic analyses of human gut tissues show reduced GDNF-RET signaling in patients with intestinal dysmotility which is associated with reduction in neural crest-derived neuronal markers and concomitant increase in transcriptional patterns specific to mesoderm-derived neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ProjectR analysis showing increased MEN-specific pattern usage in OD patients in Figure 14a.

claim: Normal intestinal function in the adult gastrointestinal tract requires an optimal balance between neural crest-derived and mesoderm-derived neuronal lineages within the ENS.
source: Normal intestinal function in the adult gastrointestinal tract therefore appears to require an optimal balance between these two distinct lineages within the ENS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing functional consequences of lineage imbalances.

claim: During fetal development, the mammalian ENS is populated by neurons and glia derived from neural crest (NC)-derived precursors.
source: During fetal development, the mammalian ENS is populated by neurons and glia derived from neural crest (NC)-derived precursors (Uesaka et al., 2016; Obermayr et al., 2013; Hao and Young, 2009; Anderson et al., 2006; Young and Newgreen, 2001; Young et al., 2000; Bergner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing this developmental paradigm.

claim: NC-derived precursors follow diverse migratory routes to colonize and innervate various parts of the gut before birth.
source: These precursors follow diverse migratory routes to colonize and innervate various parts of the gut before birth (Uesaka et al., 2015; Espinosa-Medina et al., 2017; Burns, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on ENS development.

claim: The neural crest lineage may not persist in its entirety in the adult gut, as indicated by the observed lack of expression of fluorescent reporter protein in a subpopulation of adult enteric neurons in NC-lineage-traced mice.
source: It is not clear, however, that this lineage persists in its entirety in the adult gut, as indicated by the observed lack of expression of fluorescent reporter protein in a subpopulation of adult enteric neurons in NC-lineage-traced mice (Laranjeira et al., 2011; Brokhman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior observations that motivated the current study.

claim: Alternative sources of enteric neurons that have been proposed include the ventral neural tube (VENT).
source: Alternative sources of enteric neurons that have been proposed in the literature include the ventral neural tube (VENT) (Sohal et al., 2002), or the Pdx1-expressing pancreatic endoderm (Brokhman et al., 2019), but the interpretation of these studies has been limited by the lack of robust lineage markers for non-NC derived neurons (Habeck, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research proposing alternative sources.

claim: Alternative sources of enteric neurons that have been proposed include the Pdx1-expressing pancreatic endoderm.
source: Alternative sources of enteric neurons that have been proposed in the literature include the ventral neural tube (VENT) (Sohal et al., 2002), or the Pdx1-expressing pancreatic endoderm (Brokhman et al., 2019), but the interpretation of these studies has been limited by the lack of robust lineage markers for non-NC derived neurons (Habeck, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research proposing alternative sources.

claim: The interpretation of studies proposing alternative sources of enteric neurons has been limited by the lack of robust lineage markers for non-NC derived neurons.
source: Alternative sources of enteric neurons that have been proposed in the literature include the ventral neural tube (VENT) (Sohal et al., 2002), or the Pdx1-expressing pancreatic endoderm (Brokhman et al., 2019), but the interpretation of these studies has been limited by the lack of robust lineage markers for non-NC derived neurons (Habeck, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior critique of these alternative hypotheses.

claim: Prior studies have documented cellular changes to the ageing ENS.
source: In addition, while prior studies have documented cellular changes to the ageing ENS (Saffrey, 2013), the developmental mechanisms behind these changes are unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on ENS aging.

claim: The developmental mechanisms behind cellular changes to the ageing ENS are unknown.
source: In addition, while prior studies have documented cellular changes to the ageing ENS (Saffrey, 2013), the developmental mechanisms behind these changes are unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The early post-natal ENS is derived from the canonical NC-lineage.
source: In this study, we found that while the early post-natal ENS is derived from the canonical NC-lineage, this pattern changes rapidly as the ENS matures, due to the arrival and continual expansion of a novel population of Mesoderm-derived Enteric Neurons (MENs) which represent an equal proportion of the ENS in young adulthood and with increasing age, eventually outnumber the NC-derived Enteric Neurons (NENs).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by lineage tracing data in Figure 10.

claim: Mesoderm-derived Enteric Neurons (MENs) represent an equal proportion of the ENS in young adulthood.
source: In this study, we found that while the early post-natal ENS is derived from the canonical NC-lineage, this pattern changes rapidly as the ENS matures, due to the arrival and continual expansion of a novel population of Mesoderm-derived Enteric Neurons (MENs) which represent an equal proportion of the ENS in young adulthood and with increasing age, eventually outnumber the NC-derived Enteric Neurons (NENs).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 10c showing approximately 50% MENs at P60.

claim: With increasing age, MENs eventually outnumber the NC-derived Enteric Neurons (NENs).
source: In this study, we found that while the early post-natal ENS is derived from the canonical NC-lineage, this pattern changes rapidly as the ENS matures, due to the arrival and continual expansion of a novel population of Mesoderm-derived Enteric Neurons (MENs) which represent an equal proportion of the ENS in young adulthood and with increasing age, eventually outnumber the NC-derived Enteric Neurons (NENs).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 10c showing ~96% MENs at P510.

claim: The NEN population is regulated by glial-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) signaling through its receptor RET.
source: We also found that, while the NEN population is regulated by glialderived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) signaling through its receptor RET, the MEN population is regulated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing GDNF effects on NEN populations in Figure 10k.

claim: The MEN population is regulated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) signaling.
source: We also found that, while the NEN population is regulated by glialderived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) signaling through its receptor RET, the MEN population is regulated by hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) signaling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HGF effects on MEN populations in Figure 10l.

claim: Increasing HGF levels during maturation or by pharmacological dosing increase proportions of MENs.
source: Increasing HGF levels during maturation or by pharmacological dosing increase proportions of MENs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 10f, j, and l showing HGF effects.

claim: Decrease in GDNF with age decrease NENs.
source: Similarly, decrease in GDNF with age decrease NENs; and increasing GDNF levels by pharmacological dosing increase NENs proportions in the adult ENS to impact intestinal motility.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10e, g, h showing age-dependent GDNF decline.

claim: Increasing GDNF levels by pharmacological dosing increase NENs proportions in the adult ENS to impact intestinal motility.
source: Similarly, decrease in GDNF with age decrease NENs; and increasing GDNF levels by pharmacological dosing increase NENs proportions in the adult ENS to impact intestinal motility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 10k and 13 showing GDNF treatment effects.

claim: The mesoderm is an important source of neurons in the second largest nervous system of the body.
source: These results indicate for the first time that the mesoderm is an important source of neurons in the second largest nervous system of the body.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The increasing proportion of neurons of mesodermal lineage is a natural consequence of maturation and aging.
source: The increasing proportion of neurons of mesodermal lineage is a natural consequence of maturation and aging; further, this lineage can be expected to have vulnerabilities to disease that are distinct from those affecting the NEN population.
evidence: This is based on the age-dependent changes in lineage proportions shown in Figure 10.

claim: The mesodermal lineage can be expected to have vulnerabilities to disease that are distinct from those affecting the NEN population.
source: The increasing proportion of neurons of mesodermal lineage is a natural consequence of maturation and aging; further, this lineage can be expected to have vulnerabilities to disease that are distinct from those affecting the NEN population.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the distinct developmental origins and molecular profiles of the two lineages.

claim: In Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice, tdTomato is expressed by all derivatives of Wnt1+ NC-cells.
source: We analyzed small intestinal longitudinal muscle-myenteric plexus (LM-MP) from adult (post-natal day 60; P60) Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice, in which tdTomato is expressed by all derivatives of Wnt1+ NC-cells (Becker et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the expected behavior of the lineage tracing mouse model, supported by citation.

claim: GFAP was always co-expressed with tdTomato in Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice.
source: In these tissues, while GFAP, a glial marker, was always co-expressed with tdTomato (Figure 1a), tdTomato-expression was absent in many myenteric neurons (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: tdTomato-expression was absent in many myenteric neurons in Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice.
source: In these tissues, while GFAP, a glial marker, was always co-expressed with tdTomato (Figure 1a), tdTomato-expression was absent in many myenteric neurons (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1b and 1c.

claim: Almost half of all myenteric neurons expressing the pan-neuronal marker Hu did not express the tdTomato reporter in P60 Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice (44.27±2.404 SEM).
source: By careful enumeration, almost half of all myenteric neurons expressing the pan-neuronal marker Hu were found to not express the reporter (percent tdTomato- neurons: 44.27±2.404 SEM; enumerated from 2216 neurons from six mice, Figure 1d).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration of neurons shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Myenteric ganglia in Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice contain tdTomatohigh and tdTomatolow neurons.
source: In these lineage-traced mice, myenteric ganglia were found to contain tdTomatohigh and tdTomatolow neurons and due care was taken to image subsets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This describes the observation of variable reporter expression shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Both tdTomatohigh and tdTomatolow neurons were classified as tdTomato+ and only neurons that did not show any tdTomato-expression were classified as tdTomato- neurons.
source: Both tdTomatohigh and tdTomatolow neurons were classified as tdTomato+ and only neurons that did not show any tdTomato-expression were classified as tdTomato- neurons.
evidence: This describes the classification criteria used for data analysis.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining using antibodies against tdTomato protein showed a consistent lack of reporter expression in a population of myenteric neurons.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of small intestinal LM-MP tissue from adult Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice using antibodies against tdTomato protein showed a consistent lack of reporter expression in a population of myenteric neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This confirms the observation using antibody-based detection shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The lack of reporter expression is not a function of tissue peeling or fixation, as tdTomato- cells were also observed in freshly harvested unpeeled gut tissue.
source: This lack of reporter expression is not a function of tissue peeling or fixation, as the tdTomato- cells within the myenteric ganglia were also observed in freshly harvested unpeeled gut tissue, when imaged using a live tissue fluorescence microscope (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in supplementary figure to rule out technical artifacts.

claim: Myenteric ganglia of Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice show tdTomato aggregation in cells from both freshly harvested and immediately fixed tissue.
source: In addition, we noticed that myenteric ganglia of the Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato transgenic mouse show similar tdTomato aggregation in cells of the myenteric plexus from both freshly harvested and immediately fixed tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d, e).
evidence: This observation is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Cells that show hyper-aggregation of tdTomato are in advanced stages of cell death.
source: Since we previously showed ongoing neuronal loss in healthy ENS (Kulkarni et al., 2017), we reasoned that cells that show hyper-aggregation of tdTomato are in advanced stages of cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior published work and current observations.

claim: Cells with hyper-aggregation of tdTomato showed a lack of staining for the nuclear marker DAPI.
source: Cells with hyper-aggregation of tdTomato showed a lack of staining for the nuclear marker DAPI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), suggesting that these are indeed cells in the advanced stages of death, and given that they are not labeled with antibodies against Hu, their presence does not alter our estimation of tdTomato-expressing neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is observational data shown in supplementary figures supporting the cell death interpretation.

claim: Mesoderm-derived cells during embryogenesis express Tek.
source: Mesoderm-derived cells during embryogenesis express Tek (Bardot et al., 2017) and analysis of LM-MP tissues from adult male Tek-Cre:Hprtlsl-tdTomato lineage-traced mice revealed the presence of a population of tdTomato+ neurons (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on Tek expression.

claim: Analysis of LM-MP tissues from adult male Tek-Cre:Hprtlsl-tdTomato lineage-traced mice revealed the presence of a population of tdTomato+ neurons.
source: Mesoderm-derived cells during embryogenesis express Tek (Bardot et al., 2017) and analysis of LM-MP tissues from adult male Tek-Cre:Hprtlsl-tdTomato lineage-traced mice revealed the presence of a population of tdTomato+ neurons (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is observational data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Tek is not expressed in the adult ENS.
source: Since Tek is not expressed in the adult ENS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), the presence of Tek-derived adult myenteric neurons suggested their mesodermal origin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunolabeling data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The presence of Tek-derived adult myenteric neurons suggests their mesodermal origin.
source: Since Tek is not expressed in the adult ENS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), the presence of Tek-derived adult myenteric neurons suggested their mesodermal origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental expression pattern of Tek.

claim: Mesoderm posterior 1 (Mesp1) is a definitive developmental marker for the embryonic mesoderm.
source: We then used mesoderm posterior 1 or Mesp1 as a definitive developmental marker for the embryonic mesoderm (Chan et al., 2013; Devine et al., 2014; Lescroart et al., 2014; Klotz et al., 2015) to confirm the mesodermal derivation of the non-NC derived adult enteric neurons.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing Mesp1 as a mesodermal marker.

claim: tdTomato was expressed in about half of all myenteric neurons in P60 Mesp1Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato lineage-traced mice (50.28±2.89 SEM).
source: Analysis of small intestinal LM-MP from P60 Mesp1Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato lineage-traced mice showed that tdTomato-expression was observed in about half of all myenteric neurons (Figure 2f; percent tdTomato+ neurons: 50.28±2.89 SEM; enumerated from 484 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The S46 antibody was raised against the slow tonic myosin heavy chain protein MHCst derived from avian embryonic upper leg muscle.
source: Because of the variable expression of the reporter gene in the transgenic mice described above, we also labeled tdTomato+ neurons in the myenteric plexus of Mesp1Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice with the S46 antibody, which was raised against the slow tonic myosin heavy chain protein MHCst derived from avian embryonic upper leg muscle, and is expressed exclusively by mesoderm-derived cell populations (Figure 2g; Sokoloff et al., 2007; Stockdale and Miller, 1987; Miller et al., 1985; Vaughan et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the antibody used, supported by citations.

claim: MHCst is expressed exclusively by mesoderm-derived cell populations.
source: Because of the variable expression of the reporter gene in the transgenic mice described above, we also labeled tdTomato+ neurons in the myenteric plexus of Mesp1Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice with the S46 antibody, which was raised against the slow tonic myosin heavy chain protein MHCst derived from avian embryonic upper leg muscle, and is expressed exclusively by mesoderm-derived cell populations (Figure 2g; Sokoloff et al., 2007; Stockdale and Miller, 1987; Miller et al., 1985; Vaughan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: MHCst immunostaining was exclusively observed in all Tek-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato+ MENs.
source: MHCst immunostaining was exclusively observed in all Tek-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato+ MENs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is observational data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: None of the 107 MHCst+ intra-ganglionic cells observed across three Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice expressed tdTomato.
source: None of the 107 MHCst+ intra-ganglionic cells observed (35.67±6.17 SEM MHCst+ cells per mouse) across three Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice expressed tdTomato, suggesting that MHCst immunostaining was exclusive to non-NC lineage neurons (Figure 2h, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a shows the same image where the MHCst immunostained ganglia can be observed with and without the tdTomato channel for better visualization).
evidence: This is quantitative observational data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: MHCst immunostaining was exclusive to non-NC lineage neurons.
source: None of the 107 MHCst+ intra-ganglionic cells observed (35.67±6.17 SEM MHCst+ cells per mouse) across three Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice expressed tdTomato, suggesting that MHCst immunostaining was exclusive to non-NC lineage neurons (Figure 2h, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a shows the same image where the MHCst immunostained ganglia can be observed with and without the tdTomato channel for better visualization).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of co-expression with NC marker.

claim: Both lineage tracing and protein biomarker expression provide strong support for the mesodermal origin of MENs.
source: Thus, both lineage tracing and protein biomarker expression provides strong support for their mesodermal origin (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The two distinct lineages (NENs and MENs) together account for all the adult small intestinal myenteric neurons.
source: Along with our observations on Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice (Figure 1c), our results indicate that these two distinct lineages together account for all the adult small intestinal myenteric neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementary proportions of the two lineages.

claim: RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that transduces GDNF signaling in NC-derived enteric neuronal precursors.
source: The proteins RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase that transduces GDNF signaling in NC-derived enteric neuronal precursors, and MET, a receptor for hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), are expressed by different subsets of adult myenteric neurons (Avetisyan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RET function, supported by citation.

claim: MET is a receptor for hepatocyte growth factor (HGF).
source: The proteins RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase that transduces GDNF signaling in NC-derived enteric neuronal precursors, and MET, a receptor for hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), are expressed by different subsets of adult myenteric neurons (Avetisyan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MET function.

claim: RET and MET are expressed by different subsets of adult myenteric neurons.
source: The proteins RET, a receptor tyrosine kinase that transduces GDNF signaling in NC-derived enteric neuronal precursors, and MET, a receptor for hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), are expressed by different subsets of adult myenteric neurons (Avetisyan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: MET is classically expressed by mesoderm-derived cells.
source: MET is classically expressed by mesoderm-derived cells (Rappolee et al., 1996), and by using immunostaining of small intestinal LM-MP tissues from Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato and Mesp1Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice, we found that the expression of MET was restricted to a sub-population of adult MENs (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on MET expression.

claim: The expression of MET was restricted to a sub-population of adult MENs.
source: MET is classically expressed by mesoderm-derived cells (Rappolee et al., 1996), and by using immunostaining of small intestinal LM-MP tissues from Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato and Mesp1Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice, we found that the expression of MET was restricted to a sub-population of adult MENs (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: RET expression was confined to NENs.
source: By contrast, RET expression was confined to NENs (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Inhibitory enteric motor neurons express the nitric oxide-producing enzyme nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS1).
source: In the current paradigm regarding the neurochemical basis for the functional classification of adult enteric neurons, inhibitory enteric motor neurons express the nitric oxide-producing enzyme nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS1), excitatory motor neurons express the acetylcholine-producing enzyme choline acetyl transferase (ChAT), and enteric sensory neurons, called intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) express the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) (Bergner et al., 2014; Avetisyan et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the current paradigm for ENS neuron classification, supported by citations.

claim: Excitatory motor neurons express the acetylcholine-producing enzyme choline acetyl transferase (ChAT).
source: In the current paradigm regarding the neurochemical basis for the functional classification of adult enteric neurons, inhibitory enteric motor neurons express the nitric oxide-producing enzyme nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS1), excitatory motor neurons express the acetylcholine-producing enzyme choline acetyl transferase (ChAT), and enteric sensory neurons, called intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) express the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) (Bergner et al., 2014; Avetisyan et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the current paradigm for ENS neuron classification, supported by citations.

claim: Enteric sensory neurons, called intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs), express the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP).
source: In the current paradigm regarding the neurochemical basis for the functional classification of adult enteric neurons, inhibitory enteric motor neurons express the nitric oxide-producing enzyme nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS1), excitatory motor neurons express the acetylcholine-producing enzyme choline acetyl transferase (ChAT), and enteric sensory neurons, called intrinsic primary afferent neurons (IPANs) express the neuropeptide calcitonin gene related peptide (CGRP) (Bergner et al., 2014; Avetisyan et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the current paradigm for ENS neuron classification, supported by citations.

claim: Both tdTomato+ NENs and tdTomato- MENs express NOS1, ChAT, and CGRP.
source: Immunostaining using antibodies against NOS1, ChAT, and CGRP in the LM-MP from P60 Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice showed that both tdTomato+ NENs and tdTomato- MENs express these neuronal markers (Figure 3d, f and h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3d, f, and h.

claim: The majority of NOS1+ inhibitory neurons are NENs (72.94% NENs vs 27.06% MENs).
source: Quantification of proportions in these neuronal lineages shows that the majority of NOS1+ inhibitory neurons and ChAT+ excitatory neurons are NENs (Figure 3e; of the 616 NOS1+ neurons observed across three mice, NOS1+ tdTomato-: 27.06%±4.46 SEM; p<0.0001; Fisher's exact test)
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The majority of ChAT+ excitatory neurons are NENs (73.66% NENs vs 26.34% MENs).
source: (Figure 3g; of the 912 ChAT +neurons observed across three mice, ChAT+ tdTomato-: 26.34%±2.54 SEM; p<0.0001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The majority (~75%) of CGRP+ neurons are MENs.
source: By contrast, the majority (~75%) of CGRP+ neurons were found to be MENs (Figure 3i; of the 146 CGRP+ neurons observed across three mice, CGRP+ tdTomato-: 75.76%±0.63 SEM; p<0.0001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The mean cell size of MENs (17.47±0.50 SEM µm Feret diameter) was significantly larger than that of NENs (13.03±0.36 SEM µm).
source: Apart from their derivation from a distinct developmental lineage, the mean cell size of MENs was significantly larger than that of NENs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a; n=143 neurons/group observed across three mice; Feret diameter (µm) MENs: 17.47±0.50 SEM, NENs: 13.03±0.36 SEM, p=0.002; Student's t-test).
evidence: This is quantitative morphometric data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Unbiased and agnostic clustering of scRNAseq data from tissues of two 6-month-old adult male C57BL/6 wildtype mice identified clusters of NC-derived cells by exclusive expression of canonical NC markers Ret and Sox10.
source: We performed truly unbiased and agnostic clustering of the scRNAseq data from tissues of two 6-month-old adult male C57BL/6 wildtype mice (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, c). We identified clusters of NC-derived cells by exclusive expression of canonical NC markers Ret and Sox10 (which include the clusters of Ret-expressing NENs and Sox10-expressing Neuroglia); and the MENs cluster by its co-expression of the genes Calcb (CGRP), Met, and Cdh3 (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This describes the scRNAseq analysis approach and results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The MENs cluster was identified by its co-expression of the genes Calcb (CGRP), Met, and Cdh3.
source: We identified clusters of NC-derived cells by exclusive expression of canonical NC markers Ret and Sox10 (which include the clusters of Ret-expressing NENs and Sox10-expressing Neuroglia); and the MENs cluster by its co-expression of the genes Calcb (CGRP), Met, and Cdh3 (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify the MENs cluster in scRNAseq data.

claim: 1,737 NC-derived cells across the NENs (77 cells) and Neuroglia (1660 cells) clusters were compared with 2223 cells in the MENs cluster.
source: With cells from both samples pooled together, we compared 1,737 NC-derived cells across the NENs (77 cells) and Neuroglia (1660 cells) clusters with 2223 cells in the MENs cluster.
evidence: This provides quantitative information about the scRNAseq dataset composition.

claim: Enzyme-based dissociation methods are unequally tolerated by diverse cell types, which is known to cause over- or under-representation of several cell types in scRNAseq.
source: It is important to note here that it is well known that enzyme-based dissociation methods are unequally tolerated by diverse cell types, which is known to cause over- or under-representation of several cell types in scRNAseq (Uniken Venema et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about scRNAseq methodology, supported by citations.

claim: The relative sizes of the NENs and MENs clusters in the scRNAseq data should not be taken as a reliable indicator of their actual proportions in tissue.
source: Thus, the relative sizes of the NENs and MENs clusters in the scRNAseq data should not be taken as a reliable indicator of their actual proportions in tissue.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpreting scRNAseq data based on known technical limitations.

claim: MENs express neuronal marker genes Elavl2 (HuB), Hand2, Pde10a, Vsnl1, Tubb2b, Stmn2, Stx3, and Gpr88.
source: We found detectable expression of genes Elavl2 (HuB), Hand2, Pde10a, Vsnl1, Tubb2b, Stmn2, Stx3, and Gpr88 in the MENs as well as in the NC-derived cell clusters (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The expression of neuronal marker genes Pde10a, Vsnl1, Gpr88, Stx3, and Tubb2b by enteric neurons has not been previously studied.
source: While expression of Elavl2, Stmn2 and Hand2 has been previously observed in enteric neurons (Heanue and Pachnis, 2006; D'Autréaux et al., 2007), the expression of neuronal marker genes Pde10a (expressed by medium spiny neurons in the striatum Strick et al., 2010), Vsnl1 (expressed by hippocampal neurons Bernstein et al., 2002), Gpr88 (expressed by striatal neurons Massart et al., 2009), Stx3 (expressed by hippocampal neurons Soo Hoo et al., 2016), and Tubb2b (expressed by adult retinal neurons Breuss et al., 2015) has not been studied.
evidence: This identifies novel findings about gene expression in enteric neurons, with citations for expression in other neuronal types.

claim: The MENs cluster was enriched in previously characterized ENS markers, such as Ntf3 and Il18.
source: In addition, the MENs cluster was also enriched in previously characterized ENS markers, such as Ntf3 and Il182,63 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: More than 40 neuronally significant genes were detected whose expression was unique to or enriched in MENs scRNAseq cluster.
source: In addition, we also detected >40 neuronally significant genes whose expression was unique to or enriched in MENs scRNAseq cluster, when compared with other larger cell clusters of macrophages, smooth muscle cells, neuroglia, and vascular endothelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Decorin (Dcn) is a gene coding for a chondroitin-dermatan sulphate proteoglycan, which is expressed by mesoderm-derived cells, including fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells.
source: Decorin (Dcn) is a gene coding for a chondroitin-dermatan sulphate proteoglycan, which is expressed by mesoderm-derived cells, including fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells (Neill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Decorin, supported by citation.

claim: Decorin was found to be highly expressed in the MENs cluster.
source: Decorin was found to be highly expressed in the MENs cluster in our data (Figure 5a), and not by the neurons in the Zeisel et al. database (Figure 5b; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Decorin is not expressed by neurons in the Zeisel et al. database.
source: Decorin was found to be highly expressed in the MENs cluster in our data (Figure 5a), and not by the neurons in the Zeisel et al. database (Figure 5b; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published scRNAseq data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: DECORIN protein is expressed specifically by tdTomato-negative small intestinal myenteric neurons of the Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato lineage fate mapping mouse.
source: We used a validated antibody against DCN (Scott et al., 1993) and found that this protein, known to be specifically expressed by mesoderm-derived cells, is expressed specifically by tdTomato-negative small intestinal myenteric neurons of the Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato lineage fate mapping mouse (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: At P11, MENs were found only in few isolated myenteric ganglia and represented only ~5% of all myenteric neurons (4.12%±2.98 SEM).
source: At P11, MENs were found only in few isolated myenteric ganglia (Figure 10a) and together represented only ~5% of all myenteric neurons (tdTomato- neurons: 4.12%±2.98 SEM; n=1327 Hu+ neurons counted from three mice), suggesting that they originate shortly before this age.
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration shown in Figure 10.

claim: MENs originate shortly before P11 age.
source: At P11, MENs were found only in few isolated myenteric ganglia (Figure 10a) and together represented only ~5% of all myenteric neurons (tdTomato- neurons: 4.12%±2.98 SEM; n=1327 Hu+ neurons counted from three mice), suggesting that they originate shortly before this age.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low proportion of MENs at P11.

claim: By P22, MENs account for ~30% of all neurons (29.63%±1.229 SEM).
source: The proportion of MENs in myenteric ganglia rises sharply thereafter: by P22, they account for ~30% of all neurons (tdTomato- neurons: 29.63%±1.229 SEM; n=742 neurons counted from three mice)
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration.

claim: At P60, MENs represent ~45% of all neurons (46.38%±4.62 SEM).
source: and at P60 they represent ~45% of all neurons (tdTomato- neurons: 46.38%±4.62 SEM; n=700 neurons counted from three mice).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration.

claim: At P180, MENs continue to represent roughly half of all myenteric neurons (57.29%±3.62 SEM).
source: During the adult ages, the proportions of MENs in the adult ENS remains relatively stable as at P180, MENs continue to represent roughly half of all myenteric neurons (tdTomato- neurons: 57.29%±3.62 SEM; n=586 neurons counted from three mice).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration.

claim: At the very old age of 17 months (P510), the ENS is populated almost exclusively by MENs (95.99%±1.62 SEM).
source: However, MENs dominate the proportions of the aging ENS as at the very old age of 17 months (P510), the ENS is populated almost exclusively by MENs (Figure 10b; tdTomato- neurons: 95.99%±1.62 SEM; n=996 neurons counted from three mice).
evidence: This is quantitative data from enumeration shown in Figure 10b.

claim: GDNF-RET signaling is responsible for proliferation and neurogenesis from NC-derived ENS precursor cells during development as well as for the survival of Ret-expressing enteric neurons.
source: GDNF-RET signaling is responsible for proliferation and neurogenesis from NC-derived ENS precursor cells during development as well as for the survival of Ret-expressing enteric neurons (Gianino et al., 2003; Natarajan et al., 2002; Taraviras et al., 1999; Rodrigues et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: HGF signaling has been shown to be essential for the proliferation of mesoderm-derived cells.
source: Similarly, HGF signaling has been shown to be essential for the proliferation of mesoderm-derived cells (Amano et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GDNF protein levels are markedly reduced between the P10 and the P30 ages and remains reduced thereafter up to the P90 age.
source: We found that in agreement with a previous report (Amano et al., 2002), GDNF protein levels are markedly reduced between the P10 and the P30 ages and remains reduced thereafter up to the P90 age (Figure 10g; n=3 mice/age-group, F=6.821, DFn, DFd = 1, 7, p=0.0348, One-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 10g.

claim: Expression of Gdnf transcripts show significant reduction between the ages of P30 and P90.
source: In addition, expression of Gdnf transcripts show significant reduction between the ages of P30 and P90 (Figure 10h; n=6 mice/age-group, P30: 1.070±0.179 SEM, P90: 0.539±0.129 SEM, p=0.037, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data shown in Figure 10h.

claim: HGF expression increases progressively between P10 and P90 ages.
source: On the other hand, HGF expression increases progressively between P10 and P90 ages (Figure 10i and j: n=3 mice/age-group, Protein levels: F=8.820, DFn, DFd = 1, 7, p=0.02; mRNA levels: F=36.98, DFn, DFd = 1, 16, p<0.0001, One-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is based on western blot and qPCR data shown in Figures 10i and j.

claim: GDNF treatment promoted the juvenile phenotype by enhancing the proportions of tdTomato+ NENs and correspondingly reduced the proportion of tdTomato- MENs in P20 mice to a level similar to that seen at the P10 age.
source: On administration of GDNF or saline to cohorts of P10 Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice over 10 days 87,96, we found that GDNF treatment promoted the juvenile phenotype by enhancing the proportions of tdTomato+ NENs and correspondingly reduced the proportion of tdTomato- MENs in P20 mice to a level similar to that seen at the P10 age, while retaining the MENs proportions in saline-treated control mice remained at a level expected of its age (Figure 10k; Controls: %MENs: 25.87±4.37 SEM of 1350 neurons from three mice; GDNF: %MENs: 3.86±0.07 SEM of 1301 neurons from three mice; p=0.0072; Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from GDNF treatment shown in Figure 10k.

claim: The GDNF-driven expansion of NENs and associated contraction of MENs conserved the total neuronal numbers.
source: Consistent with a previous report Gianino et al., 2003, the GDNF-driven expansion of NENs and associated contraction of MENs conserved the total neuronal numbers (Figure 10k; Controls: neurons/ganglia = 20.60 ± 4.00 SEM; GDNF: neurons/ganglia = 24.39 ± 6.96 SEM; p=0.52; Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on quantification data shown in Figure 10k.

claim: HGF administration to cohorts of P10 Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice over 10 days promoted an increase in the tdTomato- MENs population in P20 mice to levels previously observed in P60 mice.
source: HGF administration to cohorts of P10 Wnt1-Cre:Rosa26lsl-tdTomato mice over 10 days promoted an increase in the tdTomato- MENs population in P20 mice to levels previously observed in P60 mice, while tissues from saline-treated control mice exhibited a MENs:NENs ratio that is expected at P20 (Figure 10l; Controls: %MENs: 27.40 ± 5.49 SEM of 1970 neurons from 5 mice; HGF: %MENs: 49.37 ± 5.52 SEM of 1704 neurons from five mice; p=0.02, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from HGF treatment shown in Figure 10l.

claim: HGF treatment did not cause any significant change in total neuronal numbers.
source: Similar to GDNF treatment, HGF treatment also did not cause any significant change in total neuronal numbers (Figure 10l; Controls: neurons/ganglia = 20.35 ± 2.22 SEM; HGF: neurons/ganglia = 18.21 ± 0.69 SEM; p=0.38, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on quantification data shown in Figure 10l.

claim: Ret+/- mice show a significant reduction in the proportions of Ret-CFP+ NENs between 9 weeks and 16 weeks of age.
source: Using antibody against CFP/GFP to detect CFP+ RET-expressing neurons, we found that Ret +/-mice show a significant reduction in the proportions of Ret-CFP+ NENs (Figure 12b; 9 weeks: %CFP+ neurons: 24.91±5.42 SEM of 837 neurons from three mice; 16 weeks: %CFP+ neurons: 13.13±0.98 SEM of 1227 neurons from five mice; p=0.03, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on quantification data from Ret+/- mice shown in Figure 12b.

claim: A corresponding significant increase in the proportions of MHCst+ MENs with age was observed in Ret +/-mice.
source: We observed a corresponding significant increase in the proportions of MHCst+ MENs with age in Ret +/-mice (Figure 12c; 9 weeks: %MENs: 58.74±7.33 SEM of 644 neurons from three mice; 16 weeks: %MENs: 82.84±3.58 SEM of 935 neurons from five mice, One-way ANOVA, p=0.014)
evidence: This is based on quantification data from Ret+/- mice shown in Figure 12c.

claim: Control Ret+/+ mice showed no significant age-associated change in the proportions of MENs between 9 and 16 weeks.
source: while control Ret+/+ mice showed no significant age-associated change in the proportions of MENs (Figure 12c; 9 weeks: %MENs: 43.27±3.24 SEM of 780 neurons from three mice; 16 weeks: %MENs: 54.48±4.07 SEM of 1276 neurons from five mice, One-way ANOVA, p=0.36)
evidence: This is based on quantification data from control mice shown in Figure 12c.

claim: 16 week old Ret +/-mice displayed significantly delayed intestinal transit compared to age-matched control Ret+/+ mice.
source: Consistent with a prior report (Gianino et al., 2003), 16 week old Ret +/-mice displayed significantly delayed intestinal transit compared to age-matched control Ret+/+ mice (Figure 12d; WGTT (in min) Ret+/+: 121.4±4.01 SEM; Ret+/-: 157.3±14.62 SEM, p=0.048; Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on whole gut transit time measurements shown in Figure 12d.

claim: GDNF treatment caused significant improvement in intestinal transit in 17-month-old mice.
source: While the two cohorts showed no significant difference in their intestinal transit times at baseline (WGTT (in min) Control: 192.8±11.55 SEM; GDNF: 202.4±7.60 SEM, p=0.50, Student's t-test), GDNF treatment caused significant improvement in intestinal transit (Figure 13a, WGTT (in min) Control: 175.0±8.89 SEM; GDNF: 101.0±8.91 SEM, p=0.0004, Student's t-test), reaching levels previously observed in healthy mice (Figure 12d).
evidence: This is based on whole gut transit time measurements in aged mice shown in Figure 13a.

claim: GDNF treatment significantly reduced the proportions of MHCst+ MENs in 17-month-old mice.
source: GDNF treatment significantly reduced the proportions of MHCst+ MENs (Figure 13b; Figure 13—figure supplement 1a, b; Control: %MENs: 88.76±1.48 SEM of 909 neurons from five mice; GDNF: %MENs: 74.12±5.98 SEM of 799 neurons from five mice; p=0.045; Student's t-test)
evidence: This is based on quantification data from GDNF-treated aged mice shown in Figure 13b.

claim: GDNF treatment increased the numbers of RET+ NENs in 17-month-old mice.
source: while increasing the numbers of RET+ NENs (Figure 13c; Figure 13—figure supplement 1c, d; Control: RET+ neurons: 1.35±0.05 SEM in forty-two 40 X fields from four mice; GDNF: RET+ neurons: 3.19±0.56 SEM in forty-one 40 X fields from four mice, p=0.017; Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on quantification data from GDNF-treated aged mice shown in Figure 13c.

claim: GDNF treatment did not change the average neuronal numbers in the ileal myenteric ganglia of 17-month-old mice.
source: Consistent with our earlier observation, GDNF treatment did not change the average neuronal numbers in the ileal myenteric ganglia (Control: 17.56±1.82 SEM neurons per ganglia, GDNF: 16.01±1.22 SEM neurons per ganglia, p=0.49, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on quantification data from GDNF-treated aged mice.

claim: Two of the four MENs-specific NMF-patterns showed significantly higher usage in OD samples compared to controls.
source: This projection analysis indicated that two of the four MENs-specific NMF-patterns showed significantly higher usage in OD samples compared to controls (Figure 14a, Figure 14—figure supplement 1; Student's t-test, p<0.05), providing evidence that the enteric neuropathy in these patients is associated with a relative increase in MENs-specific transcriptional signatures.
evidence: This is based on ProjectR analysis of human patient data shown in Figure 14a.

claim: In addition to Gdnf and Ret, other important NEN genes (Snap25 and Nos1) were significantly downregulated in OD patients.
source: We further queried the differential gene expression analysis performed by Kim et al and found that in addition to Gdnf and Ret (as reported by them) other important NEN genes (Snap25 and Nos1) were also significantly downregulated while the MEN marker genes identified in this study (Clic3, Cdh3, Slc17a9) (Figure 14b) were significantly upregulated.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 14b.

claim: MEN marker genes (Clic3, Cdh3, Slc17a9) were significantly upregulated in OD patients.
source: We further queried the differential gene expression analysis performed by Kim et al and found that in addition to Gdnf and Ret (as reported by them) other important NEN genes (Snap25 and Nos1) were also significantly downregulated while the MEN marker genes identified in this study (Clic3, Cdh3, Slc17a9) (Figure 14b) were significantly upregulated.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 14b.
